Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The morning arrives not as a revelation but as a quiet negotiation between light and the curtains. I lie still for a moment, listening to the refrigerator hum its single note, the neighbor’s dog answer with a sleepy bark, and the first car swish past the window like a secret being kept from the street. There is no urgency in this room, only the slow inventory of ordinary things: a glass of water, a book face-down, the blue chair holding yesterday’s coat. I think about how much of life is indeed made from such small survivals and daily quiet reparations.

On the table beside the bed, the glass of water holds a small trembling sky. I lift it and drink, and the sky disappears. This is how memory works sometimes: you hold a moment carefully, then you swallow it, and it becomes part of your body’s weather. Last night I dreamed of a house I have never lived in, its hallways lined with doors that opened onto other hallways. In the dream I was not lost. I was simply walking, opening each door, greeting the rooms as if they were old friends. And asking quietly after their old ghosts today.

Words are strange little animals. They arrive when called, but sometimes they refuse to sit still. I say “home” and see a yellow kitchen; you say “home” and see a locked door. We use the same sound to carry different weathers. This is why arguments can happen in the same language and still be translations. Last week I tried to explain a feeling to a friend and ended up describing the sound of rain on a tin roof. She nodded. That was enough. We did not need to agree on the roof, or even on the rain itself at all.

Later I walk to the corner café, where the barista knows my order but not my name. This arrangement suits us both. She draws a heart in the foam, though not for me especially; it is simply what the milk does when her wrist turns. I sit by the window and watch the city perform its morning routine: bicycles threading through traffic, a woman dragging a red suitcase, a man arguing with a parking meter as if it owed him money. Nobody looks happy, exactly, but nobody looks hopeless either. We are all practicing our lives in public together daily.

At noon the light turns blunt and honest. Shadows shrink under parked cars. I buy a pear from a street vendor and eat it on a bench, juice running to my wrist. A pigeon watches with the patience of a creditor. Across the street, construction workers shout over the drilling, their voices rising and falling like a flock. I think about time, how it is both a river and a habit. We say we “spend” it, as if it were money, but no one has ever shown me the account. Still, I feel the balance shrinking and I hurry anyway.

In the afternoon I visit my grandmother. She is ninety-three and remembers the name of every dog she has ever met, but not what she ate for breakfast. “The dogs,” she says, “were important.” We sit on her porch while she tells me about a collie named Ranger who followed her to school every day for six years. She describes the exact shape of his ears. She does not remember her wedding anniversary. I decide this is not a failure of memory but a hierarchy of love. The dogs were important. I hold her hand and ask about Ranger’s bark.

By evening the sky has become a bruised peach. I walk home through the park, past the fountain that has been dry for two summers. Someone has drawn a chalk sun on the pavement and written underneath: WE ARE HERE. The chalk is already fading. A child runs through the imaginary water and laughs anyway. I sit on a bench and let the day settle. It is easy to believe that meaning must be grand, but most of it is this small: a remembered dog, a pear, a chalk sun, a hand held on a porch while the light goes soft.

That night I dream I am building a house out of sentences. Each wall is a paragraph, each window a question. The roof is made of promises I have kept and promises I have broken, shingled together so tightly I cannot tell which is which. Inside, the rooms are full of people I have loved. Some are still alive. Some are not. No one is sad. They are all busy arranging furniture, arguing about where the light should fall. When I wake, I write down one sentence: Leave a door open for the unexpected guest. Then I make coffee slowly.

The coffee is bitter because I forgot to rinse the filter. I drink it anyway. Outside, a garbage truck grinds its gears, and the neighbor’s dog begins again. I think about attention, how it is the only currency that buys a life. We can spend an hour scrolling through other people’s victories and feel poorer, or spend five minutes watching steam rise from a cup and feel rich. I choose the steam. It curls and vanishes, curls and vanishes, teaching patience without words. This is not transcendence. It is Tuesday. Tuesday will never come again. Still, it is enough today.

Tomorrow I will forget this. That is the arrangement. The pear will become a vague sweetness; the dog’s name may slip; the chalk sun will wash away in the next rain. But the day will have been lived, which is different from solved. I will make more coffee. I will forget to rinse the filter. I will walk past the dry fountain and see whatever is written next. Maybe, in the middle of an ordinary hour, I will remember that attention is a form of prayer, and that a Tuesday can still be holy if you stay long to notice.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical day-in-the-life reflection uses small sensory details to explore memory, attention, and ordinary meaning.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gentle and observant, finding emotional weight in a glass of water, a pear, a grandmother’s remembered dog, and coffee made imperfectly. Its pathos comes from the recognition that these moments fade, paired with the choice to attend to them anyway. The prose invites the reader to slow down and treat noticing—not solving or achieving—as a way of living.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample repeatedly foregrounds ordinary objects and routines as vessels for meaning: water, weather, coffee, a chalk sun, a dry fountain, and the remembered dog Ranger. Memory is selective and fragile, but the text presents that selectivity tenderly, as a “hierarchy of love.” Its central moral claim is that attention can make an ordinary day feel sufficient, even sacred.

## Evidence line
> I think about attention, how it is the only currency that buys a life.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample has a coherent, recurring investment in attention and everyday tenderness, expressed through specific images rather than an abstract thesis alone.
